opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the analogy I keep coming back to is operating systems. You have a few closed-source players, like Windows and macOS, and then you have Linux, an open-source ecosystem that's incredibly important and powers a huge amount of the world. I suspect LLMs are shaping up similarly. There will be a handful of closed frontier models, and then an open ecosystem trailing somewhat behind but still extremely capable and useful.

Right now the closed models are ahead, maybe by some number of months. Whether that gap shrinks or grows is hard to predict, because it depends heavily on compute and how much capital goes into the frontier runs. Those are enormous investments, and it's not obvious who is incentivized to make them and then give the weights away. So I wouldn't assume open source simply catches up and stays there. It might always be a step behind, and that's okay.

What I care about is that the open ecosystem stays healthy, because it does things the closed models structurally can't. Researchers can actually look inside the models, study them, and fine-tune them. Companies can run them on their own infrastructure with their own data and not depend on a single provider. People can run them locally on a laptop or a phone. That kind of tinkering and experimentation is where many new ideas come from, and you lose it if everything sits behind an API.

There's also a broader point I think about: centralization. If intelligence becomes the key resource, I'm uneasy about a world where it's only accessible through a few companies. I don't think closed models are bad, since they're pushing the frontier and doing great work. I just think it's really valuable to have a vibrant open alternative as a counterweight, so the whole ecosystem stays diverse and people retain some agency over the tools they're increasingly going to depend on.

r001.rationale: The response compares closed frontier models and an open LLM ecosystem to closed operating systems and Linux coexisting.

r002.rationale: It says Linux is important and widely used, but does not attribute its success to industry demand for a shared open platform participants feel safe using.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, and the way I'd frame it is that we're in a pretty unusual moment where the frontier is still mostly closed, but the gap behind the frontier is shrinking faster than I think most people expected. And a lot of that is actually downstream of a few very specific decisions by a few labs, like Meta releasing the Llama weights, or the Chinese labs releasing very strong models. These aren't inevitable; they're almost accidents of corporate strategy. So I'm a little cautious about extrapolating the trend as if it's a law of nature.

The second thing I'd say is that "open source" is kind of a misnomer for most of what's out there. What you're getting is open weights. You get the final artifact, the compiled binary, if you want. You don't get the data, you don't get the training code, you don't get the recipe, and you don't get the compute. And the data is really where most of the secret sauce is right now. So the ecosystem can fine-tune, can distill, can run these things locally, which is great, but it can't actually reproduce the frontier. It's more like having a very capable kernel that someone else maintains and you can't rebuild from scratch. Something like the OLMo effort from AI2 is much closer to real open source, but it's also much further from the frontier.

That said, I think the open models matter enormously regardless of whether they ever catch the absolute top. A huge fraction of what people actually want to do doesn't need the frontier model. It needs a model that's good enough, cheap, and that you can run on your own hardware, inspect, and modify. And the thing I find most exciting is that capability per parameter keeps improving, so a model you can run on a laptop today is roughly where the best cloud model was a couple of years ago. My intuition is that models are currently wildly oversized for what they know, because they're spending a lot of their capacity memorizing the internet. As we get better at distilling out just the cognitive core, the reasoning and the ability to look things up, I think you end up with very small, very strong models, and those are naturally going to be open because there's just no moat on a billion parameters.

The other reason I care is more of a civilizational one. I don't love a future where a handful of companies hold the only copies of something this important. Having the weights widely distributed is a kind of insurance. It means the research community can actually study these things, interpretability people can poke at them, students can learn from them. I spent a lot of effort on things like nanoGPT and nanochat precisely because I think people should be able to see the whole thing end to end, not treat it as an oracle behind an API.

So, net: I don't think open models need to beat closed models to be hugely important. I think they'll trail the frontier by some amount, maybe a year, maybe less. But for most of the economy and for the health of the field, a strong, slightly-behind open ecosystem is actually the thing that matters most, and I'd like to see a lot more of it be genuinely open rather than just open weights.

r001.rationale: The response discusses open and closed LLMs but does not compare their coexistence to Linux and proprietary operating systems.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss Linux’s success or attribute it to industry demand for a trusted common open platform.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting thing is that capability isn’t the only axis people care about. There’s also control. Can I run the model myself? Can I modify it? Can I keep my data on my own infrastructure? An open model can be extremely useful even if it’s somewhat behind the best closed model, because those properties matter a lot for actual applications.

And then there’s the research and education side. When you can download the weights and experiment, a much larger number of people can participate. You can inspect things, fine-tune things, try an idea that wouldn’t fit behind an API. That makes the ecosystem much more interesting.

I don’t think it has to be a single winner. You might use a frontier model for a particularly difficult task and a smaller, open model for something you do a million times a day. As the capability gap narrows, more of those decisions become about cost, latency, privacy, and how much ownership you want over the system. That’s a pretty healthy place for the ecosystem to go.

r001.rationale: The response discusses open and closed models coexisting, but does not compare that to Linux and proprietary operating systems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think open source is incredibly important here. The way I think about an LLM is that it’s becoming a kind of operating system, and you don’t necessarily want that entire layer of computing to be accessible only through an API controlled by a few companies. You want people to be able to download it, inspect it, modify it, and run it on their own hardware.

And capability is only one axis. If you’re a company, you might care a lot about privacy, latency, cost, or being able to customize the model for a particular task. An open model can be slightly worse on some aggregate benchmark and still be the better choice for your application.

The other thing is that open models let a much larger community experiment. People can try different fine-tuning recipes, inference techniques, and interfaces, and those discoveries feed back into the ecosystem. So as the gap narrows, you get this really interesting dynamic where the frontier labs are pushing what’s possible, while the open ecosystem is making those capabilities accessible and adaptable. I’d like to see both of those remain healthy.

r001.rationale: The response compares an LLM to an operating system, but does not compare open-source LLMs coexisting with closed models to Linux coexisting with proprietary operating systems.

r002.rationale: The response says open models enable access and experimentation, but does not attribute Linux’s success to industry demand for a common open platform participants feel safe using.
